equation.name: Heat from radioactive rock inside a world
equation.formula:
t = max(age, 0)
L2 = ln(2)
l1 = L2 / hU8
h1 = u * ppb * sU8 * exp(l1 * t_sun) * r * qU8 * exp(-l1 * t / Gyr)
l2 = L2 / hU5
h2 = u * ppb * sU5 * exp(l2 * t_sun) * r * qU5 * exp(-l2 * t / Gyr)
l3 = L2 / hTh
h3 = th * ppb * sTh * exp(l3 * t_sun) * r * qTh * exp(-l3 * t / Gyr)
l4 = L2 / hK
h4 = kp * ppm * sK * exp(l4 * t_sun) * k * qK * exp(-l4 * t / Gyr)
H = h1 + h2 + h3 + h4

k.name: potassium-40 the star inherited, against the Sun's

r.name: uranium and thorium the star inherited, against the Sun's

H.name: heat made in each kg of rock

source.text: Turcotte, D. L. and Schubert, G. 2014, Geodynamics, 3rd edn, Cambridge University Press

explain.curious: Rock is very slightly radioactive. Uranium, thorium and potassium-40 warm every kilogram of a planet's mantle by a few trillionths of a watt, and over a whole world that is enough to keep volcanoes and drifting continents going for billions of years. Young worlds run hotter, and a star born with more thorium gives its planets a longer-lived fire.
explain.science: Four long-lived isotopes. Today's bulk silicate Earth budget is wound back to the Sun's birth, scaled by the star's inheritance (K-40 for potassium; r-process for uranium and thorium, which are made in neutron-star mergers and some supernovae), then decayed to the body's age. U-235 and K-40 dominate in the first billion years, thorium in the far future. This is the radiogenic part only: Earth also loses about as much again as primordial heat.

references: McDonough, W. F. and Sun, S.-s. 1995, Chemical Geology 120, 223: the composition of the Earth (bulk silicate Earth U 20.3 ppb, Th 79.5 ppb, K 240 ppm). doi:10.1016/0009-2541(94)00140-4

explain.curious: The radioactive elements shun iron, so almost all of them sit in the rocky mantle and crust, not the core.
explain.science: Uranium, thorium and potassium are lithophile: they partition into silicate, so the heat-producing mass is the silicate shell (mantle plus crust).

P.name: radioactive heat of the whole world

source.text: KamLAND Collaboration (Gando, A. et al.) 2011, Nature Geoscience 4, 647

explain.curious: Earth's rocks make about 20 terawatts of heat, roughly the whole of humanity's power use. Geoneutrinos, ghost particles from those decays, let physicists weigh it directly.
explain.science: Heating per kg times the silicate mass. KamLAND and Borexino geoneutrino counts put Earth's U and Th power at 20 (+9/−9) TW, and K-40 adds about 4 TW; this budget's U and Th part (about 16.5 TW today) is inside that range.

references: Spherical geometry: heat flow is power over surface area, e.g. Turcotte and Schubert 2014, chapter 4. doi:10.1017/CBO9780511843877

q.name: heat leaving each square metre of ground

source.text: Turcotte, D. L. and Schubert, G. 2014, Geodynamics, 3rd edn, Cambridge University Press

explain.curious: Spread over the surface, Earth's radioactive heat is only a few hundredths of a watt per square metre, ten thousand times less than sunlight. Small worlds have more surface for their volume, so they cool and die first.
explain.science: Power over area. A smaller body has a larger area to volume ratio, so the same rock gives a lower flux; this is why the Moon and Mars froze geologically before Earth.

equation.name: Heat leaking up through an ice shell

q.name: heat carried up through the ice

source.text: Ojakangas, G. W. and Stevenson, D. J. 1989, Icarus 81, 220

explain.curious: Ice is a blanket. The heat leaking up from below sets how thick the ice can be before the water under it would freeze.
explain.science: Steady conduction through ice Ih whose conductivity falls as 1/T, integrated across the shell. The base sits at the freezing point of the water below. No convection: thick shells convect and carry more heat.
